1:
Gill takes the opening as a commission to compose a doleful ditty of the kind used at funerals, so as to represent the lamentable state of the nation and its governors. Henry hears the same order but locates the grief precisely: what is to be bewailed is the fall of a royal family that had long made a great figure by virtue of the covenant made with David and his seed, so that the eclipsing of it is justly lamented by everyone who knows what value to put on the covenant of God. He notes that the kings of Judah are here styled princes of Israel because their glory was diminished until they were no more than princes, and their purity lost, since they had grown corrupt and idolatrous like the kings whose ways they learned. And he draws a rule for preachers out of the commission: a minister who boldly foretells destruction must yet bitterly lament it, for we cannot expect others to be affected with what we are not affected with ourselves.

Calvin sets the parable's purpose differently, as an assignment of blame. Under the image of a lion the prophet informs us that whatever evils befell the Israelites could not be imputed to anyone else, and Calvin explains why the Spirit should insist at length on a matter not very obscure: nothing is more obstinate than the pride of men, who even under chastisement, and while pretending humility and modesty, swell with pride and bitterness and can scarcely be brought to confess that God is just and that they deserved his hand.

Who the mother is divides them. Gill denies she is the royal house of David only, or Jerusalem as the metropolis, and makes her the whole body of the people, citing the Targum's rendering of her as the congregation of Israel. Ellicott agrees that the mother stands for the whole national community, the theocracy, represented since the captivity of the ten tribes by Judah, whose princes of David's line were the legitimate kings of the whole nation. Wesley keeps all three senses together, the land of Judea, the chief city of it, and the royal family. Clarke divides them between the figures, making Judea the mother and Jerusalem the lioness. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the whole chapter with Israel as the lioness who brought up young lions among lions whose whelps, showing their leonine nature, were taken captive and led away.

Her lying down among lions is read two ways. Clarke and Wesley take it politically, for confederacy and familiarity with the neighbouring kings, since lion here means king; Wesley adds that though chosen of God to execute justice they soon degenerated into the fierce and ravening nature of the lioness. Calvin takes it morally, as a shameful mixture with the corruption of the Gentiles until they did not differ from them since God had chosen them as his peculiar people on the very condition that they should be separate from all the filth of the nations. On the first whelp there is no dispute — Gill, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all name Jehoahaz, whom the people of the land took and made king after his father was slain — and Clarke and Calvin agree that his reign was one of oppression, Calvin adding that his cruelty was intolerable and notorious among all the neighbouring nations, who conspired to destroy him. Of his capture, Clarke explains the pit from the practice of huntsmen who surround a portion of forest and narrow the enclosure until the beasts tread on pits lightly covered with branches and turf; Ellicott adds that the word rendered chains is literally nose-rings, which keeps up the figure of the lion, and that the opening clause alludes to the custom of assembling the neighbourhood to secure such a beast.
5:
Who the second whelp is turns out to be the chapter's sharpest dispute. Clarke, Calvin and Wesley all name Jehoiakim, and Gill supports the same identification by the reign of eleven years, which he contrasts with the three months of the brother who preceded him; Calvin adds the political circumstance, that this king was appointed by the Babylonian after he had wasted part of Egypt and possessed the whole of Judea, and that he too acted perfidiously and so was led away captive. Ellicott dissents on evidence. He grants that Jehoiakim was appointed by Pharaoh after the three months' reign of his brother, and that he was conquered and bound in fetters with the intention of carrying him to Babylon; but he died in disgrace in Jerusalem and was succeeded regularly by his son without foreign interference, so that the king actually carried away must be Jehoiachin, whose character was evil like his father's, and it is his ways that the following verses describe.

Gill reads the mother's action as the act of the whole people rather than a woman's, citing the interpretation that makes her the congregation of Israel. Clarke explains her waiting by weakness: the Jews found they could not resist with any hope of success, so the king of Egypt was permitted to do as he pleased. On the young lion's going up and down among the lions, Gill and Wesley take the lions for the kings of the neighbouring nations, with whom he was sometimes in league and sometimes in subjection,. Calvin takes it of his manner rather than his duration, holding that the phrase means his government was tyrannical, since in those regions kings were then scarcely human in their conduct and were everywhere like lions, so that this one was in every sense their ally in ferocity. Clarke puts it more bluntly still, that he became a perfect heathen and made Judea as idolatrous as any nation around it.

The clause about the desolate palaces is contested on the text itself. Gill reports that it may be rendered he knew their widows, or his own widows, whom he had made such by slaying the men to get their substance into his hands and then defiling them. Ellicott is firmer: though some authorities defend the received rendering, the word should be translated widows, and the mention of the king's violation of them is an unavoidable departure from the figure of the sort that often occurs in this prophet. Wesley keeps the palaces, explaining that by taking them he came to know the places, which are called here what he made them.

Who then combined against him is a further division. Ellicott holds that the nations stands, as in the earlier verse, for a single nation — there Egypt and here Babylon — the plural being natural since several were concerned in the history as a whole. Clarke names them severally as Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites under a king of many nations, and Wesley makes them the tributaries acting on the Babylonian's order. On the verb itself Calvin weighs two senses: since the word often means to utter a voice, some take it that the nations came with great clamour, as assailants attacking a wild beast excite one another; but since it also means to put, Calvin thinks it may properly be applied to counsel, so that they determined among themselves to take him. Gill allows both, having them call to one another and give their counsel together. Of the end, Gill describes an iron collar with hooks to which chains were fastened, and reports the opinion that the king died on the road and never reached Babylon; Clarke and Ellicott instead have him living on in prison for many years until a later reign released him, though never allowing him to return.
10:
The phrase rendered in thy blood is the hardest thing in the chapter, and the voices handle it four different ways. Clarke simply confesses himself beaten, saying he knows not what to make of the expression, and then lays out the alternatives others have taken: that it means a vine planted by the waters to produce the blood of the grape; that the text should be emended to read at a pomegranate, so that the vine was planted beside such a tree for support, which is what the Septuagint and Arabic appear to have read; or that a single letter should be altered to give thy vineyard, a reading he notes is supported by manuscripts. Ellicott agrees the phrase is obscure and has perplexed the commentators, and observes that some ancient versions and manuscripts have modified the text, but thinks that if it stands the sense is that the mother is like a vine living in the blood, that is in the life, of her children. Keil and Delitzsch avoid the difficulty by a different rendering altogether, planted by the water in thy repose.

Gill and Henry keep the received words and explain them from husbandry. Gill takes the allusion to be the practice of laying blood to the roots of vines, by which they were made more fruitful, and applies it to the royal blood from which the reigning prince descended. Henry develops the same image and gives it an edge: the vine was set in blood and watered with blood, as though the blood that had been shed were meant for the fattening of the soil, so freely was it spilt, and for a time it seemed to have that effect. From this he draws the observation that places of great wickedness may prosper for a while, and a vine set in blood may be full of branches.

Calvin uses the change of figure for a different purpose, to set the two states of the nation side by side. The Jews could not rightly weigh their present misery, he says, unless their former dignity and happiness were brought back to remembrance; they had grown callous to every evil, and though scarcely anything remained safe but Jerusalem they would not look back but were as wanton as when their affairs prospered. Wesley reads the fruitfulness concretely as children, noting that the king who died at Megiddo left four sons behind him besides other branches of the royal line.

The strong rods divide them over what is meant. Gill and Wesley take them for the many able men who rose in the nation and were fit to hold sceptres, Wesley calling them persons endowed with qualifications befitting kings. Henry makes them the magistrates, men of sense, learning and experience, branches of uncommon bulk and strength or else poles for the support of the vine, whose boughs had grown mature enough to be made into the white staves borne by rulers. Clarke narrows the reference sharply to Zedekiah and his many sons, and reads the exalted stature as that king's pride in his numerous offspring and prosperity, which persuaded him he might safely rebel against Babylon although he had copied his predecessor's example. Calvin rejects one rendering outright: those who translate it above the sceptres of rulers have not grasped the meaning, for the prophet intends that the sceptres were gathered from these very branches, or rather that the branches were so formed as to be like royal sceptres, kings being taken from the people as branches from a vine through the whole line from David to Zedekiah. On the height, Ellicott corrects thick branches to clouds and calls the expression a deliberate hyperbole for the excellence of the vine, a reading Keil and Delitzsch share in rendering the growth as ascending among the clouds.
12:
Calvin explains why the uprooting is described as sudden. Had the nation been slowly diminished the change would not have been remarkable, but a reversal accomplished in a short space ought to affect men to the quick, and the vine here is struck as by lightning, torn up, withered and burnt in an instant. Clarke fills the same clause with the events, the city taken after a violent siege by a king enraged at the breaking of an oath sworn to him, burnt to the ground, the sons of the last king killed before his eyes and his own eyes then put out before he was carried away in chains. Ellicott dates the beginning earlier, with the captivity of Jehoiachin and part of the people, and observes that although much remained to be accomplished it was now close at hand, so that the prophet speaks in the past tense as though he already saw it done. Gill traces the ruin back further still, through the Assyrian removal of the ten tribes, and finds the warning unheeded by the two that remained. Wesley reads the east wind as the king of Babylon raised up to pull up a sinful kingdom,.

On the planting in the wilderness they agree in substance and differ in what they draw from it. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take the desert for Babylon, and all three make the same point: the country itself was fertile, and it was the hardship and the cruelty of the captors that made it a wilderness to the exiles. Ellicott extends the thought past the return. Such was Babylon to Israel in its national relations, and even after the exile the Jews never rose again to much importance among the nations; but meanwhile they were being disciplined, so that at least a few of them might be prepared for the planting among them of that kingdom not of this world which was to fill the whole earth.

Calvin raises an objection against himself here that none of the others notices. The two clauses look openly at variance, since the vine is said to have been not merely withered but burnt up, and yet planted in a desert place; if it was withered it could not take root again, and the burning removes the slightest hope, for who ever saw a vine spring up and grow out of its own ashes? His answer is that the burning describes the conclusion men were bound to reach by their own senses when the city was utterly ruined, that being in truth a horrible spectacle, rather than the final state of the thing itself.

The fire that goes out of a rod of her branches is the last dispute, and it is a real one. Gill identifies the rod as Zedekiah, then on the throne, and the fire as his rebellion against Babylon and the breaking of his covenant and oath, which provoked the Lord and brought down the fire of his wrath; Wesley says the same in a line, the fire of rebellion kindled by one of the blood-royal. Clarke looks past the king altogether to Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, also of the blood-royal, who assassinated the governor left in the land, killed many and carried others off toward the Ammonites, before being pursued by the son of Kareah; and Clarke reads the closing words to mean that no one of the blood-royal was left, so that from that time not one of her own royal race ever sat upon the throne. Calvin keeps the emphasis on culpability, taking the point of the image to be that the last slaughter proceeded from the people themselves, the prophet forestalling their accustomed complaints. Wesley states the outcome plainly: the regal dignity is ceased.
